title: Ἁλιεῖς καὶ θύννος
part: The Fishermen and the Tunny (Chambry 22 · Perry 21)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 22 (= Perry 21). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἁλιεῖς ἐπ’ ἄγραν ἐξελθόντες καὶ πολὺν χρόνον κακοπαθήσαντες οὐδὲν συνέλαβον· καθεζόμενοι δὲ ἐν τῇ νηὶ ἠθύμουν.
sentences.tr: Halieis ep’ agran exelthontes kai polyn chronon kakopathēsantes ouden synelabon· kathezomenoi de en tēi nēi ēthymoun.
sentences.l: Fishermen having gone out for a catch and having suffered hardship a long time took nothing; and sitting in the boat they were disheartened.
sentences.i: Some fishermen went out after a catch, toiled a long while, and took nothing; they sat in the boat, dispirited.
sentences.n: The aorist-participle chain that opens nearly every fable here: ἐξελθόντες … κακοπαθήσαντες, two participles for what led up to the single main verb συνέλαβον. πολὺν χρόνον is an accusative of extent of time. ἄγρα is the hunt or the catch, on land or at sea. The raised dot (·) is Chambry's ano teleia, a stop heavier than a comma and lighter than a full stop.

sentences.t: Ἐν τοσούτῳ δὲ θύννος διωκόμενος καὶ πολλῷ τῷ ῥοίζῳ φερόμενος ἔλαθεν εἰς τὸ σκάφος ἐναλλόμενος.
sentences.tr: En tosoutōi de thynnos diōkomenos kai pollōi tōi rhoizōi pheromenos elathen eis to skaphos enallomenos.
sentences.l: But in the meantime a tunny, being pursued and being borne along with a great rush, escaped notice leaping into the boat.
sentences.i: Meanwhile a tunny, chased and driven on at great speed, leapt unnoticed into the boat.
sentences.n: λανθάνω carries its own participle: ἔλαθεν … ἐναλλόμενος is literally “it escaped notice leaping in,” which English has to turn round into “it leapt in unnoticed.” You will meet this reversal often. ῥοῖζος is the whistling rush of something moving fast — an arrow, a gust, here a fish in flight. What is chasing the tunny the Greek does not say.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ συλλαβόντες αὐτὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν πόλιν ἐλάσαντες ἀπημπόλησαν.
sentences.tr: Hoi de syllabontes auton kai eis tēn polin elasantes apēmpolēsan.
sentences.l: And they, having seized it and having driven to the city, sold it off.
sentences.i: They took it, rowed to the city, and sold it.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ, “and they” — the article alone resumes the fishermen, with no noun. ἐλάσαντες, from ἐλαύνω “drive,” is of a ship to drive it on with the oars. ἀπεμπολάω is to sell off, to turn into cash.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλάκις ἃ μὴ τέχνη παρέσχε, ταῦτα τύχη διεβράβευσεν.
sentences.tr: Houtō pollakis ha mē technē paresche, tauta tychē diebrabeusen.
sentences.l: Thus often, the things which skill did not furnish, these chance awarded.
sentences.i: Thus it often happens that what skill does not furnish, chance awards.
sentences.n: The relative clause comes first and a demonstrative picks it up afterwards (ἃ … ταῦτα), a Greek habit English usually reverses. παρέσχε and διεβράβευσεν are gnomic aorists: past in form, timeless in force — the ordinary tense of a proverb in Greek. The literal keeps the past form, the idiomatic gives the timeless present. διαβραβεύω is rare, properly to act as umpire and award the prize, so chance here hands the prize over. τέχνη and τύχη, craft and luck, are a standing Greek pair.
